We introduce LEATHER, a neural dialogue agent designed to generate human-like responses by leveraging a layered evaluation of textual characteristics. This approach allows the model to prioritize specific features during generation based on their importance in various conversational contexts. We demonstrate that this evaluation-based mechanism enhances sample efficiency, enabling the agent to reach performance levels comparable to a baseline model trained on a much larger dataset. Furthermore, we find that this produces more natural conversations characterized by greater lexical and syntactic diversity, appropriate turn-taking patterns, and a higher degree of relevance to previous utterances.

This study examines several recent lattice QCD studies concerning the strongly interacting particle species at finite temperature and arbitrary net baryon density. We present the current understanding regarding the rich and intricate aspects of the hot, dense early universe and the early stages of a baryon-rich heavy-ion collision.

This research introduces a statistical framework for predicting offshore wind turbine loads, utilizing chained Gaussian processes to address the sequential nature of load generation. This model accounts for the temporal hierarchy, spanning from environmental inputs to mechanical response. By employing Gaussian processes, the approach offers a robust non-parametric framework capable of characterizing both stochastic and deterministic characteristics of these time series. Validated against numerical outputs from the open-source code OpenFAST, the framework demonstrates strong predictive accuracy. Additionally, its utility as a surrogate model is explored, showing the ability to represent complex simulations efficiently while delivering high-fidelity load estimations.

This study examines a Twitter dataset collected during the magnitude 7.0 Izmir earthquake on October 30, 2020. The analysis visualizes the geographical distribution of users and their connections, alongside the linguistic characteristics of the tweets.

A group $G$ is defined as $R_\infty$ if every element in its braid group $N/[N,N]$ belongs to the rational closure. This paper constructs an infinite family of solvable Baumslag-Solier groups, denoted as $\Gamma_{m,n}=\langle a,b \mid a^nb=a^n \rangle$ for integers $1 \le n \le m$, demonstrating that each quotient $\Gamma_{m,n}/Z(\Gamma_{m,n})$ exhibits the $R_\infty$ property. Furthermore, we establish that the central extensions $E_\lambda=\langle x,y,z \mid [x,z]=\lambda z, [y,z]=z, [x,y]=z \rangle$ possess the $R_\infty$ feature when $\lambda$ is not equal to 1.

This study introduces a trajectory-based methodology for globally and robustly inverting time-resolved spectroscopic data. By employing a forward-optimization strategy, the data inversion process is converted into a parameter estimation problem. The core approach involves defining an objective function that quantifies the discrepancy between simulated and experimental spectroscopic data. Minimizing this function yields optimal parameters that characterize the system's potential energy landscape and initial quantum state. Once these parameters are determined, the system's time-evolution can be accurately reconstructed. The efficacy of this strategy is validated using simulated simulations of time-resolved spectroscopic data for the NaI molecule, demonstrating its performance through two distinct scenarios: (i) a case involving a single initial quantum state and (ii) a case featuring multiple initial quantum states.

Naturalistic Driving Data (NDD) serves as a valuable asset for developing and assessing autonomous driving technologies. However, laboratory data lacks the complexity of real-world driving, while real-world data is often scarce. This study introduces SceNDD, a new Naturalistic Driving Dataset featuring diverse scenarios across various environments. The dataset includes driving footage from multiple real-world settings: a highway, a residential area, a commercial area, a parking lot, and a construction zone. These environments encompass a wide variety of scenarios, such as lane changing, lane keeping, parking, and pedestrian monitoring. The primary objective of SceNDD is to facilitate the development and evaluation of perception and planning algorithms tailored for environments where autonomous vehicles are not yet fully operational.

We propose a new class of conformal field theories termed reflected entropy, defined at the boundary of random tensor networks and constructed via branch functions in two-dimensional conformal field theory. This reflection serves as a candidate for a boundary entanglement entropy, allowing us to formulate a refined version of the entanglement first law specifically for boundary regions. Furthermore, by defining and analyzing the properties of reflection entropy, we demonstrate its monogamy and positivity. We also establish the existence of boundary conformal field theories within this new framework, deriving reflection formulas for two-dimensional topological models and boundary variants of the Ising model.

Reconfigurable Intelligent Surfaces (RIS) have emerged as a promising technology to enhance spectral efficiency in 6G systems. This paper investigates channel estimation for RIS-assisted Orthogonal Frequency Division Multiplexing (OFDM) under two specific impairments: a defective reconfigurable surface and an incomplete cyclic prefix. We propose an Enhanced Learning Machine (ELM) based channel estimation scheme. By utilizing the inherent sparsity of the radio environment, the method transforms the estimation problem into a compressed sensing task. To further handle hardware imperfections, an error model is incorporated directly into the estimation algorithm. The study evaluates both the accuracy and computational efficiency of this ELM-driven approach, comparing it against other conventional techniques.

The non-invasive measurement of time-dependent energy levels in a quantum system is examined within the context of a closed, evolving quantum state. A novel form of the integral fluctuation theorem (IFT) for quasi-probability distributions, valid for both discrete and continuous energy spectra, is derived. This theoretical framework establishes an upper limit on the mean of the recorded random energy and demonstrates that the average information loss can never surpass the mean initial free energy. The study further reveals that the variance of the measured energy is bounded by both a term proportional to the initial free energy and the variance of the initial state itself. Additionally, a specific condition is identified that allows the measured energy variance to vanish, and the practicality of this approach is verified through numerical simulations.

We examine deformation and stability properties specific to $\mathrm{G}_2$-instantons on manifolds exhibiting nearly $\mathrm{G}_2$ geometry. By examining the Hessian of $\mathrm{G}_2$-instanton moduli spaces for such manifolds, the primary outcome demonstrates that instantons supported on nearly $\mathrm{G}_2$ structures are stable, provided this geometric framework is not unimodal. The analysis further includes a detailed examination of the $\mathrm{G}_2$-instanton moduli space associated with a star geometry.

The current global pandemic has spurred the development of contact tracing applications designed to assist public health authorities in combating the virus. These apps facilitate user check-ins and the identification of potential infections, thereby supporting the prevention of disease transmission. However, such systems rely on location data, which has raised significant concerns regarding user privacy and confidentiality. This study evaluates the confidentiality of contact tracing by analyzing both the operational mechanics and the underlying Coronavirus-SUS protocol. We demonstrate that while user anonymity is theoretically maintained, specific vulnerabilities within both the protocol and the smartphone's geolocation features could enable an adversary to compromise user identities.

Quantum neural networks (QNNs) are a developing field that aims to integrate quantum computing principles with neural architectures. This study presents a foundational framework for constructing quantum data into QNNs, introducing a novel quantum convolutional network (QCNN). The architecture involves preparing quantum states to represent convoluted data and executing the quantum Fourier transform to apply filtering operations. The research evaluates the proposed method using two scenarios: first, a synthetic case with a 1D convolutional network processing pre-existing quantum data; second, an application to the MNIST dataset where images are partitioned into patches, each corresponding to a separate quantum state.

We introduce a tool that generates ACL2 code for shallow embeddings of C, producing both proofs and certificates that a specific ACL2 program simulates a corresponding C program while maintaining semantic equivalence. Built upon a robust, extensible C-to-ACL2 translator, this tool is designed to handle complex C features, including pointers, arrays, structures, and the ability to invoke external C functions directly.

Building upon a conjecture by Ramanujan regarding Ramanujan's theorem on odd zeta values, this paper introduces a generalized version utilizing the Hurwitz zeta function that extends beyond the constraints of $\zeta(2k+1)^{-1}$. Additionally, we establish crucial auxiliary the integrals involving polylogarithms and provide multiple distinct proofs for these results.

We establish an equivariant elliptic cohomology theory that extends circle-equivariant complex K-theory. Applying this new framework, we compute the CP(V)-homology for complex vector space VP; specifically, we demonstrate that CP(V)-homomeric groups are isomorphic over Z to Z_ideal-generated by Z, where ideal I is the ideal of the elliptic curve's formal group law. This calculation reveals a novel structure in equivariant K-theory that distinguishes it from classical theories.

This paper investigates how enthusiastic casual Signal users understand Passkeys, commonly referred to as PINs. Through a comprehensive study involving 100 participants, we examined their comprehension of PIN functionality by analyzing responses to open-ended questions about Signal's help documentation and website pages. Our findings reveal that understanding among participants is shallow, with many misinterpreting the PIN as a method to recover deleted accounts or to bypass encryption. Additionally, we identify a need for more practical, actionable guidance to improve clarity. Finally, our results underscore the significance of conducting user studies within cryptography to assess real-world implementations and understand user behaviors.

This study introduces Gaussian quadrature Solar-weighted (S-GQ) for accurately calculating total daily solar radiation on inclined surfaces. The Gaussian quadrature method offers an efficient numerical integration technique that precisely determines the daily energy sum. By integrating Gaussian quadrature with precise solar-energy calculations, the S-GQ method enables precise computation of daily solar radiation on any surface orientation. The approach involves using daily total solar radiation on a horizontal surface as the integral weight and deriving equations for point-in-time irradiance. The method's accuracy was evaluated against two established integration techniques: the Hottel and Bankora methods. Results indicate that S-GQ matches the precision of the Hottel and Bankora methods while requiring significantly less computational time. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that the S-GQ method achieves the most accurate results when divided into two time intervals per day.

This paper introduces a new curvature access method for optimization that leverages a specific reduced architecture of the generalized Gauss-Newton (GGN) matrix. We demonstrate that GGN can be expressed as a concatenation of two components: a symmetric matrix, denoted as $H$, and a sparse matrix, denoted as $U$. The matrix $U$ features a block-column format with non-zero entries restricted to the first column. While the GGN is formed by combining $H$ and $U$, the matrix $H$ serves as their primary structural component. The matrix $H$ governs the GGN's intrinsic curvature properties, whereas the matrix $U$ influences curvature only in a secondary manner. This structural analysis reveals that the matrix $H$ corresponds to the GGN projected onto specific data directions. Consequently, the matrix $H$ can be effectively approximated using state-of-the-art neural tangent kernel (NTK) models, which are currently the leading frameworks for accessing such curvature. The proposed method's performance is substantiated through a series of experiments.

In many major Indo-European languages, nouns are assigned a grammatical gender that influences the usage of corresponding determiners and adjectives. This study investigates how such gender assignment shapes the contextual and context-independent utilization of gendered articles within neural linguistic models. By analyzing these patterns across three gender-marking languages—Spanish, German, and Swedish—we demonstrate that while the context-neutral embeddings of nouns fail to capture grammatical gender in any language, they do reflect it when the grammar consistently links gender to specific noun classes. Furthermore, both the contextual and context-independent representations of articles effectively encode grammatical gender across all three languages.

Object pose estimation is essential for various computer vision applications, including object detection, 3D reconstruction, and autonomous driving. However, training these systems demands extensive datasets populated with expensive, time-consuming manual annotations. This paper introduces a novel approach to zero-shot class-level object pose estimation that eliminates the need for annotated training data. By utilizing object detection models and integrating with CLIP, our method derives pose information from CLIP's image encoder. We validate this zero-shot class-level pose estimation framework using the Pascal VOC and COCO datasets, covering five different object categories. Experimental results indicate that our method surpasses current state-of-the-art solutions in zero-shot pose estimation, achieving an average AP of 20.2% on Pascal VOC and 18.2% on the COCK dataset.

Accurately predicting traffic flow is essential for urban traffic management, yet the inherent chaotic nature of flow patterns complicates forecasting, particularly in scenarios involving sparse sensor data. This study introduces a novel approach to predicting traffic flow that leverages similarity-based feature extraction. The proposed method enhances the forecasting performance of existing models by identifying and incorporating the most relevant features from an extensive traffic network, even when sparse, by utilizing a similarity graph constructed from historical flow data. The effectiveness of this sparse-sensor-friendly framework is validated through empirical analysis on both sparse and dense traffic datasets, with experimental results demonstrating significant performance gains over current state-of-the-art forecasting models.

This paper introduces VACA, a novel class of variational graph autoencoders designed for learning interventional and counterfactual distributions from observational data utilizing a structural causal model (SCM). Unlike prior methods that rely on learning a latent causal structure from unstructured data, VACA accepts a predefined SCIM input and focuses on efficiently mapping the induced interventional and counterfactual probability distributions. The framework employs two distinct variational autoencoder architectures: a structural encoder that simulates the underlying causal mechanism, and an interventional/counterfactual encoder that generates specific distributions by conditioning on intervention sets. Empirical evaluations across synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that VACA successfully recovers target target distributions while offering significant computational advantages over existing state-of-the-art methods.

The REAL-time Transient Collection (RTC) system, which operates on the LOFAR Low-frequency Array, is designed to identify and analyze fast radio transients. While the system's core processing resides at the global LOFAR center, local data collection occurs at individual sites. At the Irish node, lofarta (REALTA) serves as the local backend, handling the ingestion of RTC streams from other locations. This system manages data storage, event archiving, and user access. This article presents initial results from the Irish node's first year of operation, detailing the system's design, software implementation, and its performance regarding data throughput.

This article reviews recent machine-learning-driven advancements in the analysis of the fundamental properties of the more complex and promising Metaphotonics field. The introduction begins by briefly outlining Metaphotonics and explaining why its nonlocal character renders traditional analytical methods inadequate for addressing specific research inquiries. Furthermore, we examine how various computational learning techniques have been applied to elucidate key aspects of this domain, including magnetic induction, the creation of extraordinary optical transmission, optical manipulation, and photonic crystal structures. Finally, we outline future research trajectories and potential directions at the intersection of Metaphotonics and machine learning.

This study introduces a comprehensive dataset designed to analyze current film industry metrics alongside historical records from 1955 to the present. Our dataset encompasses 20 key variables—including pre-release attributes such as genre, director, and release date, as well as post-release indicators like social media engagement and box office revenue. Leveraging this dataset, we examine how pre-release traits influence box office performance. Our findings indicate a strong positive correlation between director popularity and opening weekend earnings, whereas the impact of social media activity proves negligible. Additionally, we assess the efficacy of various machine learning algorithms in predicting revenue, concluding that Gradient Boosting Machines (GBM) outperform other models in terms of accuracy.

This study demonstrates that auxiliary frequency regulation can enhance or worsen a power system's voltage dynamics. Using linear stability analysis, we establish that such regulation is necessary for stability under heavy load conditions. However, simulations reveal that it can inadvertently extend the duration of voltage collapse under light loading conditions. Consequently, operators must carefully assess their frequency regulation strategies to prevent exacerbating voltage collapse risks.

This paper introduces a novel framework designed to model and analyze the cyber-physical (CP) "network of networks" (NoN) within intelligent environments. Our approach constructs a multi-layered network architecture where each layer represents a specific domain: physical, wireless, wired, or computational. These domains are interconnected via two distinct types of links. Firstly, physical connections exist between nodes across different layers, such as between a sensor and a gateway. Secondly, logical connections form between devices within the same layer, exemplified by the relationship between gateways and servers or among servers themselves.

We define the resulting CP NoN as a complex system characterized by tight integration between its physical and cyber components, featuring multiple interaction levels and diverse communication protocols. To address critical challenges like resilience and security, we propose a dedicated intelligence layer. This layer employs machine learning and data-driven techniques to monitor and optimize the system's performance. Consequently, our comprehensive model enables the evaluation of key performance indicators (KPIs), including latency, bandwidth, and energy consumption, while also quantifying the system's resistance to both physical and cyber threats.

This paper utilizes the MAPPIES Monte-Carlo code to analyze the origin of the UV/soft X-ray excess in blazar spectra, a phenomenon attributed to inverse Compton scattering of externally polarized light. The study examines three scenarios: (i) emission from a spherical region surrounding the jet, (a) a jet component, and (b) a moving jet component. The findings reveal that all three cases can reproduce the observed excess, though the specific parameters required vary across the scenarios.

The Hough transform serves as a fundamental technique for terrain analysis, enabling the detection of planar features such as planar structures and mineral deposits, fault lines, and landslides. Nevertheless, its application is typically restricted to flat areas or regions with smooth topography due to reliance on local approximations. In this study, a new approach is introduced that extends Hough transform capabilities to analytically handle arbitrary terrains. This is achieved by employing Zernike polynomials to fit the three-dimensional topography of the area. A critical advantage of using Zernike polynomials is their ability to yield a closed-form solution for calculating the local Hough transform, thereby facilitating Hough transform operations over complex landscapes.

Helioseismic travel time measurements are fundamental for characterizing solar interior flows, yet they remain susceptible to contamination from surface activity. This study investigates how such activity influences north-south travel time data, specifically by examining the impact of shifting around active regions (AARs) on the background flows used to derive travel times. We conducted this analysis by tracking the AAR-associated flows themselves and by comparing travel time results between the original data and data cleaned of AAR surroundings. The investigation reveals that the shifts around AARs are primarily longitudinal and latitudinally stable. Furthermore, we observed a strong correlation between the travel time perturbations and the vorticity of the regional flows induced by active areas. In most instances, the travel time delays are consistent with the advection of these around-AAR flows. Additionally, the magnitude of the travel time perturbations correlates with the intensity of the AAR. Ultimately, comparing the processed and uncleaned data demonstrates that removing AAR contributions is essential for obtaining precise travel time measurements.

This study investigates stochastic gravitational waves generated by primordial electromagnetic fields within the early universe. We analyze the spectrum for cases where the initial field strength is either sub-dominant or dominant relative to the radiation content. Specifically, we examine two scenarios: one where the field decouples from expansion and transitions to the electromagnetic phase around $T_{\rm FD}\sim 100$ MeV, and another where the confinement occurs later at $T_{\rm FD}\sim 1$ MeV. In both instances, the resulting stochastic gravitational waves span a frequency range of $10^{-4}$ to $10^{-1}$ Hz, making them accessible to the LISA Pathfinder-derived Pulsar Timing Array Network.

Light field technology has garnered significant interest in recent years due to its capacity to capture both spatial and angular data of a scene. While recent advancements in neural light field compression have demonstrated impressive results, they often struggle with generalizability and real-world applicability. This study introduces a disparity-aware model specifically designed to compress arbitrary light field data in a practical manner. By integrating disparity-awareness into the compression framework, our approach effectively leverages prior knowledge of video disparity to enhance performance. The core of our method comprises two key components: a specialized disparity-aware feature extraction module and a disparity-conscious feature fusion layer. The latter functions by adaptively weighting features derived from both angular and disparity perspectives based on the specific disparity characteristics of each layer, thereby optimizing feature integration. Experimental evaluations confirm that our method delivers state-of-the-art performance for practical neural light field compression, surpassing existing approaches in both the UCF101 and KITTI data sets.

This paper evaluates both design-based and model-based strategies for generating small-area estimates within low- and middle-income countries, utilizing data from the 2016 Demographic and Health Survey in Malawi. A design-based framework employing linear mixed models utilizes survey weights to align with the survey's sampling strategy, while a model-based framework utilizes linear mixed models that decouple the sampling mechanism from the analysis model. By analyzing these approaches side-by-side using linear regression on health service utilization data, we demonstrate that model-based methods yield superior precision and lower bias levels compared to design-based alternatives. Consequently, model-based techniques offer significant potential for enhancing the accuracy of small-area estimation in developing nations.

This study investigates the electronic and optical characteristics of stacked two-dimensional materials with the general formula $MA_2Z_4$ ($M$ = Mo, W, Ti; $A$ = Si, Ge; $Z$ = N, P, As). These materials feature a unique atomic configuration where a single metal layer is intercalated between a $A_2Z_2$ monolayer and $AZ_3$ monolayer. Our results indicate that the quasiparticle band alignment in these van der Waals heterostructures is determined by the specific elemental composition rather than the layer stacking order. This unique band arrangement facilitates the generation of stacking-independent excitonic peaks in the optical absorption spectrum.

The rare decay process $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$ was recently investigated by the LHCb collaboration, which reported an initial observation of this event. However, the analysis suffered from a low signal-to-background ratio and a substantial systematic uncertainty. In contrast, the present study utilizes the LHCb detector's full 2018 data set, encompassing $6\,\text{ab}^{-1}$ of integrated luminosity. This expanded dataset enables a significantly more sensitive analysis, allowing the rare decay to be observed with $5.1$ standard deviations. The measured upper limit on the production cross-section is $1.1 \times 10^{-7}$, a figure that is $2.6$ times smaller than the previous bound established by the LHCb collaboration.

The formation of planetary systems relies on protoplanetary disks, yet current theories struggle to explain their origin. This study revisits that question by utilizing the 3D Smoothed-Particle-Hydrodynamics (SPH) code, RAMSES-DISK, to model the disk's creation during the collapse of a pre-stellar core. We focus on a 1 solar mass core collapsing under its own gravity, incorporating a protostellar outflow and a protoplanetary disk formation scenario. Our results indicate that the resulting disk possesses a mass of approximately 0.01 solar masses, with a radius of roughly 10 astronomical units, and exhibits a significant mass deficit in its outer regions. These findings suggest that the instability triggered by the outburst of a Class 0 protostar is a primary mechanism for disk formation, effectively explaining their existence despite the challenges posed by external torques.

Atmospheric models are indispensable tools for characterizing exoplanets, and their fidelity is paramount for the success of the upcoming James Webb Space Telescope. This study utilizes ground-based on-sky observations of the hot Jupiter WASP-33b to assess various atmospheric models. We analyzed 100 transits of WASP-33b to generate a high-precision light curve, which we then compared against forward modeling results using four distinct atmospheric models: (1) a model with no atmospheric absorption, (2) a model assuming a Rayleigh scattering cross-section, (3) a model based on H₂O absorption, and (4) a hybrid model combining both Rayleigh scattering and H₂O absorption. Our findings indicate that the non-atmospheric model is inconsistent with our data, whereas the three models incorporating atmospheric effects fit the light curve equally well. We further evaluated these models by analyzing their impact on derived planetary parameters. While the non-atmospheric model yields a radius that is statistically inconsistent with radius measurements from the space-based TESS observations, the Rayleigh scattering, H₂O, and combined models all yield results compatible with the TESS data.

This work addresses the challenge of forecasting temporal series across an extended timeframe, such as days, weeks, or months. We introduce a new statistical model designed to capture complex, non-linear patterns while remaining adaptable to various data characteristics. The proposed approach combines multiple periodicities with a multivariate structure and is implemented using a Bayesian framework enhanced by deep learning. By employing deep networks to capture intricate interactions between variables, the model achieves high flexibility. Crucially, we utilize a variational inference method to induce sparsity within these networks. This mechanism eliminates unused non-linear features, thereby enhancing the model's interpretability and computational efficiency. We evaluate our method against several real-world datasets and benchmark it using established baseline models. The results demonstrate that our approach surpasses existing techniques in both predictive accuracy and performance. Furthermore, we provide an empirical analysis of the impact of key hyperparameters on model outcomes.

Federated Learning (FL) serves as a robust framework for privacy-preserving machine learning, as it enables the collaborative training of a global model across multiple parties without exposing raw data. Despite its advantages, FL faces significant hurdles, particularly regarding equitable learning where participants with smaller, noisier, or biased datasets may achieve inferior model performance compared to those with larger, higher-quality datasets. While Differential Privacy (DP) is widely recognized for mathematically guaranteeing privacy, the interplay between DP and pre-existing equity challenges within FL remains underexplored. This study provides a comprehensive analysis of how varying levels of privacy protection influence this equity-equity relationship in FL. We demonstrate that the disparity in model accuracy among data providers is not uniform across all privacy settings; rather, it fluctuates depending on the specific privacy parameters employed. To address these disparities, we introduce a novel algorithm called Adaptive Federated Learning with Differential Privacy (AFLDP). AFLDP dynamically adjusts privacy safeguards for each participant based on their individual data attributes, thereby simultaneously enhancing both equity and efficiency. Empirical evaluations across multiple datasets confirm that our method outperforms existing state-of-the-art approaches by delivering superior accuracy for the previously disadvantaged providers while ensuring stronger, personalized privacy assurances.

This study presents a novel unsupervised learning (specifically using a K-means-based) strategy to optimize the throughput of reconfigurable intelligent surface (RIS)-assisted, wireless charging networks (WCS) that may experience disruptions. In this setup, the goal is to maximize the information transmission rate from a base station to an energy-harvesting user equipment (UE), where the BS transmits data signals and an additional access point provides a harvested wireless power link to the UE. Due to the presence of the RIS, the system operates within a three-dimensional structure, and the wireless power wireless transmission rate is disrupted by the presence of the RIS. To address this, the unstructured learning method is employed to cluster the UE into clusters based on the received power at the BS and the harvested power at the UE. The cluster centers are then used to determine the phase shifts of the UE, which are then used to optimize the throughput of the UE. The proposed unsupervised learning method is shown to be more effective than the traditional supervised learning method in optimizing the throughput of the UE.

This study reports a new beta-minus decay half-life measurement for $^{186}$Hg, utilizing high-purity germanium (HPGe) gamma-ray spectroscopy alongside low-background high-efficiency proportional counter techniques for the detection of pure beta-minus emissions. The gamma-ray spectrum reveals 10 distinct transitions, with the most intense occurring at 736.3 keV, which feeds a specific excited state in $^{186}$Tl. Proton capture gamma-ray data confirms that the 736.3 keV line corresponds to a J$^\pi$ = 5$^-$ level in $^{186}$Tl. Consequently, the beta-minus decay of $^{186}$Hg proceeds primarily to this 5$^-$ state, resulting in a determined half-life of 1.09(13) s. This new value is approximately a factor of two shorter than the previous measurement.

Motion synthesis techniques, such as optimal control and machine learning, have proven effective for generating complex movements across various physical systems, including biological entities and robots. However, these approaches typically depend on extensive data, such as large datasets or long simulation runs, to learn a system's dynamics. In scenarios where such data is scarce, traditional methods struggle. This paper introduces a novel data-driven control approach designed to handle severe data limitations by relying on "side information"—specifically, the relative positions of the system to its environment, such as the stance configuration of a walking robot. This scalar side information is then paired with a limited set of state transitions to train a regression model that approximates the system's dynamics. These learned dynamics are subsequently integrated into a control framework, such as model predictive control (MPC), enabling the generation of sophisticated motions even when only minimal data is available. The method's validity is demonstrated through two case studies: achieving and locomotion in an underactuated swimmer, and simultaneous learning of flight and locomotion for a flapping-wing robot, all within a data-constrained setting.

Addressing knowledge graphs (KGs) as point clouds in a high-dimensional latent space, Relational Graphs (RG) maps entity embeddings based on the direction and type of the connecting relationship. This study introduces a novel method to enhance RG learning by integrating Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) with Triplet Loss. Specifically, the TRIGAN model generates entity representations aligned with the directions and types of their neighbors. It employs a discriminator trained on triplet loss to evaluate the authenticity of these representations. The model further incorporates an adversarial objective to align the generator's output distribution with the true distribution of entity features in the embedding space. Evaluated against extensive datasets, TRIGAN surpasses current state-of-the-art methods in terms of link prediction accuracy and maintains superior performance across tasks involving few-shot scenarios.

We introduce a phase-stabilization-free quantum key distribution protocol utilizing a dual-field coherent state structure. This approach encodes qubit information in two orthogonal coherent fields, distinguishing them via phase-based and photon-number-based degrees of freedom. Consequently, coherent detection naturally produces phase-coherent signals between the two encoded qubits, thereby eliminating the need for explicit phase stabilization. The protocol demonstrates resilience against photon-number-splitting attacks and can be implemented with current off-the-shelf equipment.

This study examines the dispersion properties of ionized, atomic, and photodissociation region (PDR) gas surrounding the L1448 molecular filament within the Rho Ophiuchus complex, utilizing CO emission data from the ALMA survey of Rho Ophiuchus (ALMA/ALMA Project). We find that the velocity structure of the gas is dominated by dispersion, which increases systematically from the PDR to atomic and finally to ionized phases. This observed trend in dispersion correlates with rising turbulent Mach numbers and sound speeds across these environments. Furthermore, we identify a pronounced inverse relationship between the dispersion and tidal acceleration, indicating that gravitational forces suppress turbulent motion. Consequently, the gas self-regulates its velocity against the disruptive influence of the nearby star cluster. These findings demonstrate that turbulence in ionized, atomic, and PDR gas is intrinsically linked to the phase of matter and the local intensity of gravitational tidal forces.

Transformer architectures, once a subject of academic curiosity, have recently emerged as a cornerstone for addressing complex challenges across various application domains. This paper provides a comprehensive survey of Transformer models tailored for spatial-related tasks, including computer vision and reinforcement learning. It examines the advancements made in applying Transformers to these fields, analyzes their inherent strengths and limitations, and outlines prospective research avenues. Furthermore, the study introduces a structured catalog of prominent Transformer-based models, their associated datasets, and key research initiatives within sight.

This study addresses the challenge of forecasting short-term mortality rates, which serves as a critical issue for life insurance firms. We evaluate the performance of two versions of the time-series factor model: one featuring time-varying factor loadings and another with time-homogeneous loadings. Our analysis indicates that the time-varying loading model delivers superior predictive accuracy, outperforming the traditional time-homogeneous version. Additionally, we demonstrate that the time-varying factor loadings effectively capture the second cohort effect.

Neural Architecture Search (NAS) seeks to automatically discover high-performance neural network architectures, yet the vast architectural space and prohibitive training costs remain significant hurdles. This work introduces a novel strategy to enhance NAS efficiency by mitig interferences among subtasks. We demonstrate that interference arises when subtasks are ordered sequentially, causing later jobs to inherit suboptimal policies from earlier ones. To address this, we propose a task scheduling method that leverages policy transfer to reduce inter-task interference. Furthermore, we develop an interference-aware search framework that integrates this scheduling capability with a subtask selection mechanism. This approach enables the architecture search process to adaptively choose the most promising components based on current knowledge. Experimental results across multiple NAS benchmarks validate the efficacy of this method, showing a 20% reduction in training time and a 5% improvement in accuracy compared to prior state-of-the-art solutions.

These eigenvalues are typically complex numbers with negative real parts; however, in lossless systems, they vanish entirely, whereas dissipative systems feature eigenvalues with non-zero negative real components. The study establishes that the sum of their imaginary parts is directly proportional to the total scattering phase shift. Additionally, a separate relationship is identified between these eigenvalues and the phase shift phase itself. The findings are validated through numerical simulations of one-dimensional quantum and classical scattering scenarios.

Leveraging the flexibility of neural networks, this paper introduces a novel method for optimizing the architecture of winning lottery tickets. Instead of pruning individual weights, the approach minimizes the count of operations by scribing the structure through whole convolutional layers. By utilizing a sifting algorithm based on the Boolean search problem and introducing new attributes to represent the network topology, the study demonstrates that the optimized winning tickets maintain or even surpass performance compared to standard fully linked models. Additionally, the research confirms that these streamlined networks require no manual tuning of the search parameters.

This paper introduces a methodology for valuing lottery tickets based on a decision maker's risk tolerance, utilizing the Constant Absolute Risk Aversion framework. The primary objective is to determine the ideal selling price for these games and identify the most advantageous moment for an individual to acquire a ticket. The proposed valuation technique relies on the certainty equivalent of the lottery's payoff, offering a straightforward formula for valuation that remains consistent regardless of current wealth levels. By using this constant risk-adjusted approach, we derive an explicit expression for a ticket's worth, facilitating the analysis of how risk preferences influence the optimal purchase timing. The study concludes with a numerical illustration demonstrating the practical application of this valuation method.

Valley degrees of freedom are pivotal in the physics of two-dimensional (2D) materials, with their evolution driven by diverse mechanisms. While earlier research primarily identified valley relaxation via electron-phonon scattering, this study reveals an alternative process where phonons directly cause valley hopping without intermediate electron scattering. We demonstrate that this phonon-driven mechanism is prevalent in 2D systems and can even surpass the traditional scattering route in temperature regimes below 100 K. We analyze how this overlooked process depends on material properties and phonon modes, showing that it is highly sensitive to phonon dispersion and can be orders of magnitude stronger than scattering-induced relaxation in certain materials. Furthermore, this novel mechanism offers a tunable lever for controlling valley dynamics, enabling potential extensions of valley-based spintronic concepts into the phononic domain through phononic cooling strategies.

This report outlines a winning solution to the NeurIPS 2022 Visual Domain Adaptation Challenge, which evaluates adaptation techniques across three tasks: animal image classification, vehicle part localization, and vehicle part detection. The primary difficulty stemmed from significant domain shifts characterized by the presence of coarse segmentation maps and the need to leverage this information. The proposed methodology involved a two-stage process: first, utilizing a pre-trained model to generate refined segmentation maps from these coarse inputs; second, employing a specialized domain adaptation technique to handle the final adaptation task using both the improved segmentation maps and the initial predictions. The core technique integrates a U-Net architecture with a Graph Convolutional Network (GCN) to jointly learn the graph structure and node features for adaptive transfer. This structure, where graph nodes represent input data and edges encode relationships, is optimized via a self-supervised approach. Experimental results indicate that this framework effectively mitigates domain shifts and produces high-quality pseudo-labels.

Morgan et al. introduced t-SNE, a technique for dimensionality reduction that maps high-dimensional data to a low-dimensional space, often utilizing it to visualize spherical data on the 2-dimensional manifold of the sphere. However, this approach treats spherical points as residual vectors pointing away from the sphere's surface, resulting in representation errors that escalate with larger spheres. To address this limitation, we propose a more accurate representation of spherical data derived from the manifold learning framework of Manifold Mapping Factorization (MMF). This new representation corrects inherent scaling errors, thereby enhancing the efficacy of t-SNE when applied to spherical datasets.

We find that second-order expansions are insufficient for accurately describing the polaron's ground state energy across all coupling strengths. To address this, we incorporate selected higher-order corrections, specifically the Luttinger and Kadanom-Wilson terms, achieving convergence up to a maximum coupling constant of 3. Our results indicate that including these higher-order terms allows convergence up to a coupling constant value of approximately 3. Our findings reveal that the second-order expansion fails to accurately capture ground state energy across the entire coupling constant spectrum, necessitating the inclusion of higher-order corrections like the Luttinger and Kadanom-Wilson terms to achieve convergence up to a maximum coupling constant value of approximately 3. We introduce a robust framework designed to accurately study the ground states of one-dimensional fermionic systems with high efficiency. This approach leverages the benefits of both analog and digital quantum computing methods. By utilizing continuous quantum gates to emulate the Hamiltonians of those fermionic systems, the method significantly lowers the number of discrete quantum gates required for implementation on an quantum processor. To address the limitations of digital gate techniques in optimizing variational ansatz angles, the system integrates a quantum classical hybrid algorithm. This combination allows for the precise determination of the quantum ground state even in highly correlated regimes. To demonstrate the effectiveness of this method, the study applies it to the one-hall fermionic Luttinger liquid model, emulating its interaction with an quantum computer while also evaluating the quality of various variational ansatz strategies.

This paper investigates various properties of specific polynomial sequences derived from fundamental characteristics of directed and undirected graphs. We derive recurrence relations, establish upper and lower bounds, and explore connections between different terms within these graphs. Furthermore, the work examines asymptotic behavior and identifies interactions between distinct polynomial sequences. As a consequence of these findings, we present asymptotic approximations and determine relations to other known combinatorial structures.

This text presents an abstract describing how to construct a canonical (Hitchin) link for any closed curve on a surface using its corresponding Veech arc in the curve complex. The pair consisting of this link and its projection is defined as the Veech pair; this concept is then applied to construct a family of links that converge toward the geodesic representative of a curve. The discussion further explores the connection between these links and those found within mapping class groups, as well as the relationship between Hitting canonical links and mapping tori.

This research investigates the influence of telecommuting on Scrum project outcomes. Initially, we conducted a case study examining a two-year software development project that transitioned from a co-located environment to one involving partial remote work. Subsequently, we executed a survey analyzing attitudes toward and the efficacy of this hybrid approach. Finally, we performed a regression analysis to determine the link between telecommuting and both project performance and team sentiment regarding remote arrangements. Our findings reveal that while team members generally hold positive views of working from home, Scrum teams do not achieve superior success rates or project performance when compared with scenarios where the entire team remains in the same physical location.

In 1987, Gau and Wu established the closed-form solution for the determinant of lower triangular matrices with arbitrary dimensions. Subsequently, the notion of Gauss-Wu value was broadened by the author to apply to arbitrary square matrices. The current work first derives and validates a formula for calculating the Gau-Wu value of a $4\times 4$ matrix while also outlining a formula for its arrow matrix counterpart. The derived findings have been confirmed through computations utilizing Maple.

The $v_2$ values were determined via the event plane and the multi-vector-event-technique approaches across transverse momenta (pT) of 2–6 GeV/$c$ and centralities of 0–60%. The data indicate that the $v_2$ for B mesons and that for B mesons in the semi-leptonic channel are statistically indistinguishable. Consider a Koszul dual pair of diagonal algebras, where the smaller dual serves as the ground ring for the larger algebra. Suppose the larger algebra corresponds to the cohomology ring of a topological space. This setup yields a bicomplex that generates a bicomplex of modules over the smaller, homomorphism-based ground ring. We demonstrate that the homology derived from this complex is independent of the specific choice of diagonal structure, thereby defining a new topological invariant known as the "steadfast homology." This concept generalizes the established "steadfast homology" introduced by Randal-Williams. As an application of this framework, we provide a novel proof for the existence of topologically cyclic, non-bordism-trivial manifolds featuring trivial Pontryagin rings, previously discovered by Randal-Williams using different methods.

This work investigates the performance gap between optimal and binary power levels in $K$-user interference networks. While prior research established that the Extremal GDoF advantage of binary over binary is $\Theta(K)$ for parallel Gaussian channels and $\Theta(\sqrt{K})$ for X networks, we demonstrate that this benefit holds universally for arbitrary Gaussian interference channels. Consequently, we conclude that the Extremal GDoF advantage of binary power over binary is $\Theta(K)$ for general Gaussian interference networks.

Auditing is a critical process for organizations to ensure the reliability of their accounting records. While auditing has traditionally been a manual and labor-intensive endeavor, the advent of information technology has made its automation a primary focus for researchers. This study introduces a novel intelligent auditing framework that integrates the auditing form concept analysis (AfCmA), a neural network, and the Dempster-Shafer theory of evidence. In this architecture, AfCmA serves to classify accounting accounts into functional groups, and the neural network identifies anomalies within these accounts. Subsequently, the auditing goal is achieved by utilizing the evidence theory to evaluate the risk levels of these anomalies. The efficacy of this proposed approach is validated through a case study.

This work presents a sampling technique for the Strauss point process, which is grounded in a sampling algorithm for the Simplex Strauss model developed by Biscagni et al. (2019). The approach utilizes the Stitching methodology introduced by M\"uller and Wang (2017), though the authors also present a proof that sampling is feasible for the Simplex case despite the apparent contradiction that simple edge weights theoretically preclude interactions. The authors demonstrate that the Strauss model can indeed be interpreted as a weighted combination of a Poisson process and a hard-core process. Theoretically, the method guarantees sampling accuracy, and numerical results indicate that the proposed approach is significantly more efficient than the standard Acceptance-Rejection technique.

This study examines a scale fractal space-time inspired by the Bekenstein-Mikowski-de Wit framework to analyze how Lorentz and Galilean symmetries are modified within the quantum theory domain. By applying the generalized uncertainty principle, we derive relations linking modified commutators and the associated energy-velocity and energy-momentum connections. These findings enable the derivation of both the deformed Schrödinger equation and the altered Lorentz-invariant action, establishing the latter's consistency with the fundamental commutators and uncertainty principles. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the deformation of Galilean symmetries naturally precedes Lorentz symmetries and that the impact of the modified Lorentz symmetry becomes negligible at low energy scales.

We address a general framework for creating school timetables, incorporating features like shared time slots for multiple classes and constraints on the consecutive use of shared slots. To tackle the resulting timetabling problem, we introduce a 0-0 integer programming (IP) model and a reduced IP formulation that specifically for the scenario involving an unrestricted consecutive shared slot limit. Additionally, we explore a heuristic methodology utilizing constraint programming (CP) suitable for broader application. Our computational analysis demonstrates that both IP formulations are highly effective in generating high-quality schedules, while also establishing that our restricted IP model is particularly well-suited for specific timetabling contexts.

This study introduces a reduced-order model of a monopod, which serves as a simplified representation of biological hopping mechanisms like those seen in frogs and insects. The model incorporates both the leg's spring and the soil's spring, with soil stiffness varying based on the leg's position. It utilizes the Reduced Order Model of Model Order Reduction (ROM) to account for spring interactions between the leg and the soil. The research examines how such yielding ground impacts hopping metrics, including peak velocity, peak force, and peak energy. Furthermore, it analyzes variations in leg velocity and the ratio of device mass to total system weight regarding their influence on yielding ground. The findings reveal that velocity significantly affects peak force and energy, while the mass ratio primarily influences peak velocity. The study also evaluates energy efficiency across different conditions and identifies an optimal velocity for maximum efficiency. Finally, it proposes strategies to enhance energy efficiency by adjusting leg velocity and adding mass to the system.

The Internet of Things (IoT) is rapidly expanding, with a critical focus on remote upgradability to ensure long-term reliability and security. This study evaluates mesh-based wireless protocols, specifically LoRaWAN and Zigbee, as platforms for the dependable distribution of firmware updates. By conducting a real-world analysis of a 200-node Zigbee cluster, the research assesses various strategies for incremental software deployment. The findings indicate that a distributed rollout approach yields superior performance compared to a global one, effectively mitigating issues such as packet loss, link disconnections, and delays. Ultimately, the work offers a practical roadmap for implementing LoRaWAN and Zigbee systems, enabling timely and secure updates to end-device functionality.

This study investigates the transition from many-body localization (MBL) to thermalization in a one-dimensional spin chain subjected to a disordered transverse magnetic field, utilizing a Fock-space renormalization group approach. By examining the Fock-space propagator $E_k$ as a function of momentum $k$, we observe that the transition to ergodicity commences at low-$k$ values, beginning well before the shift marking MBL-to-thermalization localization transition determined by level statistics. Specifically, the critical exponent characterizing the MBL to ergodicity evolution at low momenta is approximately 0.6, closely matching the multifractal index $\Delta_2$ derived from the same momentum dependence. These findings align with recent findings regarding Anderson localization in closed systems, underscoring a robust link between ergodic recovery and multifractality.

This study examines a search scenario where an agent must locate $k$ targets within a binary tree of depth $D$ while engaging in a two-way dialogue with an oracle. Unlike the classic model, the agent now communicates with both questions and responses, and crucially, the total count of interactions—combining inquiries and replies—is strictly capped. The oracle conceals the positions of the $k$ unknown targets, which are arranged in the tree, and must optimally resolve their full configuration within the interaction budget. We demonstrate that any search strategy capable of succeeding must have its depth bounded logarithmically relative to $k$. Conversely, we present an optimized two-way dialogue protocol that identifies all targets with both constant-time exchange (one question and one reply per target) and maintains full optimality.

Quantum machine learning (QML) has emerged as a rapidly developing field within quantum computing, aiming to harness quantum capabilities to enhance machine learning models. A critical challenge confronting QML is adversarial attack, where subtle, imperceptible alterations to input data lead to erroneous predictions by the model. This paper introduces a novel framework specifically designed to generate global adversarial instances and disturbances tailored for quantum neural networks. The proposed methodology involves formulating optimization problems to create robust adversarial examples and disturbances that successfully fool a quantum classifier while remaining indistinguishable to a human observer. The efficacy of this approach is validated against two benchmark datasets: MNIST and Fashion-MNIST.

The research investigates the Steklov spectrum of bounded domains in $\mathbb{R}^n$, where $n \geq 2$, with $n$ being an integer. It is demonstrated that when a domain is defined by a function that is sufficiently smooth and exhibits small deviations from a constant, the spectrum of the Steklov problem can be approximated using a power series in terms of the square of that deviation. This result is a direct consequence of the fact that the Dirichlet-to-Neumann operator is differentiable at the origin. Furthermore, this paper provides explicit formulas for the initial terms of that series.

Compliance constitutes a fundamental concept in compliance engineering, representing a formal method for determining whether a system's behavior adheres to the governing regulations. In compliance auditing, compliance is typically modeled as a compliance check where rules are expressed as compliance traces and regulations are defined as properties of these traces. However, compliance auditing frequently involves analyzing system logs that are not necessarily complete or well-formed traces. Consequently, this study introduces the concept of a trace segment alignment, enabling the comparison of two trace segments even when they originate from different executions. Specifically, we propose the infix alignment method, applicable when two segments are subtraces of a larger combined execution, and the postfix alignment method, applicable when one segment is a subtrace of the other. Utilizing these approaches, we develop a compliance verification method that leverages these distinct alignments. Empirical results indicate that the proposed method outperforms the traditional linear-time approach, which checks compliance on full traces, by achieving superior performance.

Accurate modeling of signal propagation in cellular networks is essential for network planning, optimization, and the deployment of emerging technologies. Traditionally, this modeling relies on stochastic models like Okumura-Hata, which depend on site-specific parameters and statistical distributions that result in reduced prediction accuracy. Alternatively, Machine Learning (ML) methods have gained traction for modeling propagation due to their ability to learn from data without prior domain knowledge, though they often require vast amounts of labeled training data and struggle with generalizing to new environments. This paper introduces a deep convolutional neural network (CNN) for modeling cellular signal propagation, utilizing geographic information system (GIS) maps and measured Received Signal Strength Indicator (RSSI) data. The study evaluates the approach across three distinct scenarios: cell tower downlink, user device uplink, and multi-user uplink configurations. Results indicate that the proposed model outperforms conventional benchmarks, including the Campbell model, in predicting RSSI levels.

Validating temporal plans is crucial for ensuring that temporal plans are correctly implemented. We introduce a systematic method for formally confirming the in-time correctness of temporal plans against an official semantic definition. Central to this approach is the concept of plan formality, which ensures that plan implementations align with their specifications. We also present the official semantics for temporal plans, which serve as a rigorous foundation for developing validation tools. To demonstrate the utility of these semantics, we provide an extensive set of validation examples that illustrate both compliant and non-compliant implementations.

Power system planners utilize expansion models to forecast future infrastructure investments. These models typically rely on granular data regarding generation costs, power demand, and network constraints; minor inaccuracies in such data can result in significant misjudgments regarding optimal technology mixes and investment pathways. This study introduces a new metric to quantify the sensitivity of model outputs to data errors, defining responsiveness as the ratio of output variation to input variation. We demonstrate that, particularly in smaller networks, this responsiveness can be exceptionally high, occasionally reaching levels that cause counterintuitive planning decisions. Such phenomena arise from model sensitivity to specific input configurations, driven by decision boundaries, non-differentiable costs, and network topologies. Ultimately, we contend that responsiveness serves as a vital characteristic for assessing power expansion models and must be considered when interpreting their results.

This paper examines a Vlasov-Poisson framework defined within confined boundaries, offering its interpretation as an autonomous ordinary differential equation (ODE) system along particle trajectories. Leveraging this formulation and known estimates for low-regularity regularities of the scalar potential, the authors establish global-in-time existence and uniqueness results for the coupled kinetic and hydrodynamic systems. Furthermore, these findings are applied to demonstrate rigorous solutions for the 1D/2D/3D Vlasov-Poisson model under confining potentials. In addition, similar models—including the 1D/2D/3D Vlasov-Maxwell and Poisson-Boltzmann equations under confinement—are analyzed for their short-time behavior.

We introduce a novel approach for identifying search queries that correspond to specific elements within conceptual hierarchies, such as ontologies. While current query localization techniques depend on matching existing searchable metadata, our method derives these from the conceptual structure itself for items lacking associated labels. To achieve this, we convert concepts into strings using their textual labels where available, or otherwise by generating descriptions via a two-stage process: initially filtering relevant information using multiple strictness metrics, then refining the output with a large language model. Evaluations across three datasets demonstrate that the STRICT method achieves superior performance compared to existing solutions.

Colloidal gels are highly attractive materials due to their tunable mechanical properties and broad range of applications, yet integrating them with additional functional traits remains a significant challenge. In this study, we introduce a tunable rheo-acoustic method that leverages ultrasonic vibrations to modulate the viscoelastic response of a thixotropic, body-centered cubic colloidal gel. We demonstrate that applying acoustic energy at specific intensities and frequencies can substantially lower the gel's viscoelastic modulus and shift its sol-gel transition boundary, thereby enhancing fluidity under shear. Furthermore, we establish that the gel's mechanical stiffness can be cycled repeatedly between solid and liquid phases through on-off acoustic actuation. These findings illustrate a pathway to creating functional, acoustically responsive soft matter systems.

Categorizing documents within the STEM (Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics) fields is a fundamental task for supporting research and education. While recent research has developed various neural network models to achieve this, there remains limited understanding of how these models actually differentiate between document types. To address this lack of interpretability, we introduce a method that leverages mathematical entity associations to make the categorization process more transparent. Furthermore, we utilize this approach to create a novel representation for STEM documents, linking mathematical concepts directly to corresponding sections in the source text. Experimental results validate our proposal, demonstrating that the generated math-code-entity-driven document embeddings are effective and yielding significant improvements over standard vectorization bas

This study introduces a new policy for the board game Go, called Stable Pairing (SP). The SP strategy prioritizes playing moves that maintain stability within a player's position. The paper details the mathematical foundations of SP and examines its behavior in several scenarios, including the basic functions of stable pairs and a broad range of complex, open-ended applications. Furthermore, we explore the connection between SP and formal game theory by demonstrating that SP provides the best response to an opponent also playing SP in stable pairing situations. This analysis yields a unique result: it is currently the first time such an equilibrium has been proven for a game theory model applied to a real-world setting.

Summary evaluation metrics are essential for comparing model outputs, especially in unsupervised settings. While prior research has primarily relied on reference-based metrics that require ideal samples, these approaches often prove inadequate for real-world applications where obtaining perfect summaries is impractical. To address this, we introduce SummScore, the inaugural reference-independent metric that leverages a cross-encoder model to evaluate summary quality. SumScore demonstrates strong correlation with human judgments, outperforming all existing public benchmarks in the dataset we tested. Furthermore, we conducted an extensive analysis of SummScore's performance across different domains and model architectures, and we implemented a user-friendly interface that enables researchers to easily compute this metric for model comparison.

We investigate a model for recovering a one-dimensional piecewise smooth signal from sparse quadratic measurements. This study establishes that our method is nearly optimal, surpassing the performance of standard techniques like total variation (TV) minimization. By developing a novel class of regularizers involving piecewise constant functions multiplied by TV, we achieve significantly sharper error bounds than traditional approaches. We demonstrate the efficacy of these new regularizers through numerical experiments, highlighting their superiority over existing methods.

Sensor fusion is a critical component of 3D object detection in autonomous driving systems, as it leverages the complementary attributes of LiDAR and camera sensors to enhance detection precision. Nevertheless, existing methods are often constrained by specific scenarios or techniques, lacking broad applicability. To address these limitations, we present BEVFusion, a robust and versatile LiDAR-camera fusion architecture. Unlike prior techniques, BEVFusion operates within a unified horizontal plane representation, enabling LiDAR point clouds and camera feature maps to interact seamlessly. This framework is both efficient and versatile: its core architecture yields state-of-the-art performance across multiple datasets and detection algorithms, while its design principles facilitate easy adaptation to novel tasks and applications. Extensive experiments confirm that BEVFusion surpasses current methods in overall reliability and versatility.

This study investigates the impact of temperature fluctuations on liquid turbulence within the dissipation zone. The analysis centers on the interaction between thermal and velocity fluctuations, specifically examining how the latter modulate the former. It is demonstrated that the spectral density of turbulent kinetic energy directly influences the spectral density of thermal turbulence disturbances. Furthermore, the study derives the relationship between thermal diffusivity and the length scales of velocity fluctuations, concluding that the former is contingent upon the latter. The research also establishes the proportionality between thermal dissipation and turbulent kinetic energy dissipation. Finally, the analysis provides the proportion between thermal fluctuations in temperature and fluctuations in velocity.

This study investigates the laser-induced thermal distribution within a liquid medium to explain the complex diffraction patterns it generates. We demonstrate that the oscillatory characteristics inherent in the modified diffusion equation are essential for accounting for the observed phenomena. Furthermore, the oscillations in the induced thermal profile are governed by a critical length scale, $l_c$, which relies on the ratio of thermal diffusivity to the optical penetration depth. Importantly, the period of the resulting diffraction patterns is determined by this same critical length scale, $l_c$, thereby varying inversely with both the wavelength of the light and the liquid's thermal conductivity.

Design dialogues involving human-computer interaction, whether text or speech, facilitate the integration of user inputs into product evolution. While current techniques can identify interactions within visual mining contexts, they fail to address contexts described purely through natural language. This study introduces a new approach to extract such language-based connections using design dialogues, leveraging interaction definitions from the UML design mining community. Specifically, the proposed method capitalizes on "conclusion robustness," a figure of speech representing how well a class withstands changes in its concluding section, as evidenced by our results, the approach effectively isolates textual mining within formal design dialogues.

H-STREAM serves as a data processing system designed to handle vast streams and preserve significant segments of their history. It functions as a high-performance, analytical complement to conventional streaming engines by offering persistent storage for stream content, thereby enabling cost-effective access to substantial historical datasets. Unlike traditional relational systems, H-STREAM supports online analytical processing (OLAP) directly on these streams and their accumulated histories. The system achieves this by executing complex analytical queries over both continuous streams and stored data using a query language that unifies the capabilities of current streaming and OLAP technologies. This paper details the architecture of H-STREAM, outlines its progress, and illustrates its capabilities through various complex query examples.

This work investigates non-resonant graphs capable of producing a single, sterile pair of top and bottom quarks via interaction with a vector boson $Z'$ that couples to both top and bottom charges. We analyze the $Z'$ lifetime in the context of its mass relative to the top quark mass ($m_Z' > 2m_t$) and derive precise decay widths for both decays into quarks and into a sterile top-bottom pair. We determine the necessary non-resonant graphs and calculate the relevant Wilson coefficients. We further constrain the $Z'$ coupling strength using constraints derived from the Tevaton and Large Hadron Collider (LHC) experiments.

Knowledge Base (KB) machines often suffer from catastrophic forgetting when learning to map a source ontology to a target one using a neural machine translation framework. To mitigate memory loss of previously seen elements, this paper introduces a duplicate mechanism that copies knowledge base components directly into the model's latent space. This augmented model maintains a dedicated duplicate layer dedicated to storing this ontology-specific information, allowing for seamless integration with existing SPARQL neural translation architectures. By jointly training both the primary model and its duplicates on a duplicate layer, a duplicate layer is created to preserve memory of previously unseen knowledge. Experiments on the ICEER9 dataset confirm that this approach is effective in preventing catastrophic forgetting without compromising translation performance.

The academic community increasingly prioritizes research visibility, driven by institutions and funders that utilize publication counts and high-impact citations to measure scholarly success. However, this surge in competition has created significant stress, especially among early-career researchers. A critical limitation of citation-based metrics is their inherent delay; they fail to capture the growing prestige of a work until years have passed, and they are unreliable for recent outputs lacking a historical citation record. In contrast, publication prestige can be assessed immediately through the venues where research is presented. This paper investigates the correlation between venue prestige and research citation rates, demonstrating that recent venue quality serves as a robust complement to citations and often predicts future citation success more accurately than past publication records. Consequently, leveraging venue-derived metrics offers a timely method for evaluating research quality and identifying high-potential recent works.

This study investigates neural network (NN) control systems, specifically validating them using behavioral type approaches. The core methodology involves constructing a formal model of the NN controller and comparing it against the actual system to ensure the real implementation adheres to the model's assumptions. To address this comparison, the paper introduces a formal model checking algorithm designed to detect violations of these NN model properties within the controller state space. Additionally, the approach is extended to scenarios involving environmental interactions, enabling the specification of desired system behaviors in the form of temporal logic formulas. By employing the proposed framework on a concrete networked controller application, the work demonstrates the ability to identify both design flaws in the NN architecture and limitations arising from complex interactions with the environment.

This study introduces a functorial algorithm designed to hierarchically group overlapping entities within a finite set. The method constructs two categorical structures: a source category representing similarity between entities and a target category that is neither monoid nor strict functor but remains dynamic. Notably, the target category is not a functor; however, the algorithm maintains dynamic consistency as similarities evolve. We establish that the algorithm produces a coherent and stable group hierarchy in response to incremental changes. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the group hierarchy is coherent and stable even when the initial grouping of entities undergoes minor perturbations. Finally, we provide an illustrative example that highlights the practical effectiveness and robustness of the method.

Restoring visual data from imperfect measurements is a critical challenge in numerous practical fields, including medical imaging, remote sensing, and image reconstruction. Conventional restoration methods typically rely on dividing images into fixed-size patches, which can introduce boundary artifacts and fail to capture the inherent tensor structures of streaming data. To address these limitations, we introduce a new approach for visual recovery streaming that utilizes tensor rings. This method operates through adaptive patch monitoring, dynamically adjusting patch sizes to optimize restoration outcomes. Furthermore, a robust tensor ring completion strategy is developed to effectively mitigate noise and other measurement irregularities. Experimental evaluations on remote sensing imagery and video streams demonstrate that the proposed system outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in both quantitative metrics and qualitative observations.

This paper establishes a novel link between the maximum weight autonomous (MWAS) problem and iterative graph standardization (IGS). Specifically, we demonstrate that IGS implicitly constructs a MWAS solution for a specific weight function derived from the graph's structure. This finding expands upon the recent work of Bader et al. [1], who introduced a standardization algorithm that maximizes the size of the maximum autonomous (MAS) problem. In addition, we prove that the IGS procedure can alternatively maximize the weight of the resulting maximum weight autonomous (MWAS) solution when arbitrary weights are supplied as input.

The emergence of graphene has driven significant progress in both fundamental and applied research. This study investigates the thermodynamic properties of single-layer graphene using density functional theory, specifically examining how carrier-based electrical tuning influences the material's heat capacity, free energy, and entropy across a range of temperatures and pressures. Results indicate that electrical regulation can modulate graphene's heat capacity, free energy, and entropy by up to 30%. These findings demonstrate that dynamic control of the monolayer's electronic population offers a powerful strategy for engineering its thermodynamic profile, thereby opening new avenues for applications in thermal management and energy technologies.

The primary objective was to determine the local magnetic field strength at the stellar surface by analyzing the cutoff frequency of the ECM radiation. The study identified three distinct flares, and the analysis of their radio spectra yielded magnetic field strength estimates of 0.70 ± 0.05 G, 0.60 ± 0.05 G, and 0.70 ± 0.05 G (note: original values were 0.70 ± 0.05 G, 0.60 ± 0.05 G, and 0.70 ± 0.05 G).
